subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
extraLines: 1. Define psychology. What are the main goals of psychology?
Psychology is the scientific study of behavior and mental processes of humans and animals.
Its main goals are to observe, describe, understand, explain, predict and control behavior
and mental processes.
2. Who founded the first psychology laboratory, where and when? Why is this
event important?
Wilhelm Wundt, a German philosopher and physiologist, established the first psychology
laboratory in 1879 at Leipzig, Germany. It is important because it marked the formal
beginning of psychology as an independent scientific discipline, separate from philosophy.
3. Write a short note on Hippocrates and his theory of humors.
Hippocrates (460-377 B.C.), regarded as the Father of Medicine, proposed the theory of
humors. He believed that the body contains four humors - blood, phlegm, yellow bile and
black bile - and that their balance determines health, temperament and behavior, while
imbalance produces illness.
4. What contribution did Alcmaeon make to early psychology?
Alcmaeon (500 B.C.), known as the father of Greek medicine, performed the first anatomical
dissection for research purposes. He believed that sensations and thoughts occur in the
brain, making him one of the earliest thinkers to locate mental life in the brain rather than
the heart.
5. Differentiate between structuralism and functionalism.
Structuralism (Wundt and Titchener) studied the structure of the mind by breaking conscious
experience into its basic elements through introspection. Functionalism (William James)
studied what the mind does and how it works, emphasizing the functions and purposes of
consciousness in helping the individual adapt to the environment.
6. What is introspection? Which school of thought used it?
Introspection is a method in which trained participants report their own conscious mental
experiences in response to a stimulus. It was the main method of the structuralist school of
thought founded by Wilhelm Wundt and developed by Edward Titchener.
7. Describe the Gestalt school of thought and its laws of perceptual organization.
The Gestalt school (Wertheimer, Kohler and Koffka) held that the whole is greater than the
sum of its parts and that perception is organized into meaningful wholes. Its laws of
perceptual organization include figure-ground, proximity, similarity, continuity, closure and
symmetry.
8. Explain Freud's structure of personality: id, ego and superego.
According to Freud, the id is the inborn, instinctive part that works on the pleasure principle;
the ego is the rational part that works on the reality principle and mediates between the id
and reality; and the superego is the conscience, acquired through socialization, which
represents society's norms and moral standards.
9. What are defense mechanisms? Explain any three with examples.
Defense mechanisms are unconscious strategies used by the ego to protect itself from
anxiety. Repression pushes disturbing wishes and memories out of conscious awareness.
Denial is refusing to acknowledge a painful reality, such as a smoker refusing to accept that
smoking caused his illness. Projection is attributing one's own unacceptable impulses to
others, and sublimation channels unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities,
such as taking up kickboxing to release anger.
10. Name and briefly describe Freud's psychosexual stages of development.
Freud proposed five stages: the oral stage (birth to about 1 year, pleasure from the mouth),
the anal stage (1-3 years, toilet training), the phallic stage (3-6 years, Oedipus and Electra
complexes), the latency stage (6 years to puberty, sexual impulses dormant) and the genital
stage (puberty onwards, mature sexuality).
11. How does the behaviorist approach explain human behavior? Name its main
figures.
The behavioral approach holds that behavior is learned from the environment through
conditioning and can be studied only through observable and measurable responses. Its
main figures are John B. Watson (founder), Ivan Pavlov (classical conditioning), B. F. Skinner
(operant conditioning) and Albert Bandura (observational learning).
12. Describe Pavlov's classical conditioning experiment and its key terms.
Pavlov paired a bell (neutral stimulus) with meat powder (unconditioned stimulus) that
naturally produced salivation (unconditioned response) in dogs. After repeated pairings, the
bell alone (conditioned stimulus) produced salivation (conditioned response). Key processes
include acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization and discrimination.
13. Differentiate between classical and operant conditioning.
In classical conditioning (Pavlov), an association is formed between two stimuli and the
behavior is involuntary and reflexive. In operant conditioning (Skinner), an association is
formed between a voluntary behavior and its consequence; behaviors followed by
reinforcement increase, while those followed by punishment decrease.
14. What is reinforcement? Differentiate between positive and negative
reinforcement, and name the schedules of reinforcement.
Reinforcement is any consequence that increases the likelihood of a behavior occurring
again. Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus; negative reinforcement removes an
unpleasant stimulus. Reinforcement may be continuous or partial, following fixed-ratio,
variable-ratio, fixed-interval or variable-interval schedules.
15. Explain Thorndike's Law of Effect.
Thorndike's Law of Effect states that responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in and
learned, so they are more likely to be repeated, while responses followed by dissatisfaction
are stamped out and less likely to recur. It became the foundation of Skinner's operant
conditioning.
16. What is learning by insight? Describe Kohler's experiment with apes.
Learning by insight is sudden problem solving that occurs when the learner perceives the
whole situation and the relationships among its parts. Wolfgang Kohler observed
chimpanzees, such as Sultan, who suddenly stacked boxes or joined sticks to reach bananas
placed out of reach, showing insight rather than slow trial and error.
17. Describe Bandura's social (observational) learning and the concept of
modeling.
Bandura proposed that much human behavior is learned by observation and imitation of
others, called modeling. A child who watches another child handle snakes without fear, or
who imitates aggressive behavior seen in a model, is showing observational learning, which
does not require direct reinforcement of the observer.
18. What did Watson's 'Little Albert' experiment demonstrate?
Watson conditioned a young child, Little Albert, to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud
noise. Albert later feared similar furry objects such as cotton balls and a Santa mask,
demonstrating stimulus generalization and showing that emotional responses can be
classically conditioned.
19. Explain the humanistic approach and Maslow's concept of self-actualization.
The humanistic approach emphasizes free will, human dignity, personal growth and the
capacity for self-reflection. It views people as basically good and in control of their lives.
Maslow placed self-actualization - fulfilling one's full potential - at the top of his hierarchy of
needs, above physiological, safety, love/belonging and esteem needs.
20. What is Carl Rogers' client-centered concept of congruence?
Rogers held that psychological health depends on congruence, the feeling of integration
between the self and the ideal self. When a person's self-concept matches his or her
experience and ideal self, the person is fully functioning; a large gap produces incongruence
and anxiety.
21. Describe the cognitive approach to psychology.
The cognitive approach focuses on how people know, understand, think about and
remember the world. It studies mental processes such as perception, attention, language,
problem solving and the schemas - organized bodies of information stored in memory - that
guide how new information is interpreted.
22. Name the main research methods used in psychology and describe any two.
Main methods include the experimental method, naturalistic observation, participant
observation, survey method, case study, archival research, content analysis and
meta-analysis. In naturalistic observation, behavior is recorded as it happens in real-life
settings without laboratory controls. In the survey method, a sample of people is asked
questions about their attitudes, opinions or behavior.
23. Differentiate between independent, dependent and confounding variables.
The independent variable is the factor the experimenter deliberately manipulates. The
dependent variable is the behavior or outcome that is measured. A confounding variable is a
potential variable, other than the independent variable, that could affect the dependent
variable and must therefore be controlled.
24. What is correlation? Differentiate between positive and negative correlation.
Correlation measures how strongly two variables are related to each other. In a positive
correlation both variables increase or decrease together, such as study time and marks. In a
negative correlation one variable increases as the other decreases. Correlation does not by
itself prove cause and effect.
25. What is a hypothesis? How is it different from a theory?
A hypothesis is a prediction stated in a way that allows it to be tested through research. A
theory is a broader, organized set of principles that explains observed facts and generates
hypotheses; experiments are conducted to test hypotheses derived from theories.
26. Describe Piaget's four stages of cognitive development.
Piaget proposed: (1) the sensorimotor stage (birth-2 years), in which the infant learns
through senses and actions with little symbolic representation; (2) the preoperational stage
(2-7 years), marked by language and egocentrism; (3) the concrete operational stage (7-11
years), in which reversibility and logical operations on concrete objects appear; and (4) the
formal operational stage (11 years onwards), in which abstract thinking develops.
27. Explain assimilation and accommodation in Piaget's theory.
Assimilation is incorporating new knowledge into existing schemas without changing them.
Accommodation is modifying an existing schema, or creating a new one, to incorporate new
knowledge that does not fit. Cognitive development proceeds through the continuous
interplay of these two processes.
28. Write a note on Erik Erikson's psychosocial theory of development.
Erikson proposed eight psychosocial stages across the lifespan, each built around a social
crisis, from trust versus mistrust in infancy to ego integrity versus despair in old age. Unlike
Freud, Erikson based development on social rather than sexual relationships and held that
development continues throughout life.
29. Differentiate between genotype and phenotype, and between dominant and
recessive genes.
Genotype is the genetic composition of a person, while phenotype is the observable
characteristics that result from it. A dominant gene expresses its trait even when paired with
a different gene; a recessive gene influences a trait only when paired with an identical gene.
30. Describe the structure of a neuron and explain synaptic transmission.
A neuron consists of dendrites, the branch-like structures that receive messages; the soma
or cell body containing the nucleus; the axon, which carries the impulse away; and terminal
buttons at its end. In synaptic transmission, information is relayed from one neuron to the
next across the synaptic gap by chemical messengers called neurotransmitters.
31. Differentiate between the central and peripheral nervous systems.
The central nervous system consists of the brain and the spinal cord. The peripheral nervous
system includes all the nerve cells and nerves outside the brain and spinal cord; it connects
the central nervous system with the sense organs, muscles and glands, and includes the
somatic and autonomic divisions.
32. Differentiate between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.
Both are divisions of the autonomic nervous system. The sympathetic system arouses the
body for defensive action, such as fight or flight, increasing heart rate and mobilizing energy
in emergencies. The parasympathetic system calms the body, slows heart rate and supports
rest and digestion. Together they perform the dual functions of arousing and calming.
33. Name the lobes of the cerebral cortex and state the function of each.
The frontal lobe is responsible for motor control, higher mental processes, judgment and
planning. The parietal lobe processes body sensations. The temporal lobe is involved in
hearing and in recognizing faces. The occipital lobe is associated with visual processing.
34. What is the endocrine system? How does it differ from the nervous system in
sending messages?
The endocrine system is a chemical communication network of ductless glands - such as the
pituitary, thyroid, pineal and gonads - that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
Its messages travel through the blood and act more slowly and for longer than the fast
electrical messages of the nervous system.
35. What problems are caused by abnormal secretion of the thyroid and pituitary
glands?
Under-secretion of the thyroid in childhood causes cretinism, while enlargement of the
thyroid due to iodine deficiency produces goiter; low thyroid secretion can also produce
anxiety-like symptoms such as irritability and tension. Excess growth hormone from the
pituitary causes gigantism, while its deficiency in childhood causes dwarfism.
36. Describe the structure of the eye and the functions of its main parts.
The cornea is the clear, transparent protective coating over the front of the eye. The iris, the
band of muscles behind the cornea, gives the eye its color and controls the size of the pupil.
The lens focuses light by accommodation, changing its shape to keep images sharp. The
retina contains the visual receptors - rods for dim light and black-and-white vision, and
cones, concentrated in the fovea, for color vision and fine detail. The blind spot is where the
axons of the ganglion cells leave the eye as the optic nerve.
37. Trace the path of sound through the ear and name the types of hearing
impairment.
Sound passes through the eardrum, then the three tiny bones of the middle ear - hammer,
anvil and stirrup - then the oval window and the cochlea, from where signals reach the brain.
Conduction deafness results from problems in conducting vibrations to the cochlea, such as
damage to the middle-ear bones, and can often be helped by hearing aids or microsurgery.
Nerve deafness results from damage to the neural mechanism or the auditory cortex itself.
38. Differentiate between sensation and perception.
Sensation is the process by which sensory receptors receive and represent stimulation from
the environment. Perception is the cognitive process of recognizing, organizing and
interpreting sensory information so that it becomes meaningful; it involves selection,
organization and interpretation.
39. Explain the monocular and binocular cues of depth perception.
Monocular (pictorial) cues can be seen with one eye and include relative size, interposition
(one object overlapping another), texture gradient, linear perspective and motion parallax.
Binocular cues require both eyes: retinal disparity, in which the greater the difference
between the two retinal images the closer the object seems, and convergence of the eyes.
40. What are altered states of consciousness? Give examples and name the two
categories of dream content described by Freud.
Altered states of consciousness are states that differ markedly from ordinary waking
consciousness; examples include daydreaming, meditation, intoxication, sleep and hypnosis.
Freud described two categories of dream content: manifest content, the obvious and
apparent content of the dream, and latent content, its hidden underlying meaning, which
expresses unconscious wishes, thoughts and conflicts.
